RagShortTexts: Prussian resistance beginning in 1242 brought prolonged conflict with the Order.
The 1249 Christburg settlement concerned particular groups and conditional rights and duties.

Variants.Content: Resistance beginning in 1242 brought parts of Prussia into prolonged warfare with the Order, affecting castles, villages and supplies. At Christburg in 1249, Pomesanians and groups from Warmia and Natangia made commitments involving baptism and obedience and received arrangements concerning property, inheritance and judgement. Negotiators represented particular communities; neighbours retained grievances of their own. Some remember recovered relatives, others lost land and new duties.

The Order and local leaders need to establish consent and responsibility. Arbitrarily changing land or service after securing cooperation makes other chiefs doubt whether negotiation will protect their followers.

Men guarding or besieging castles remember provisions, wounds and captives. Peace still requires escorts for return and exchange. One result does not make every village along a route willing to supply them.
Damaged households ask whether they can return to fields, who collects dues and who recognises family property. Baptism can change access to negotiations without supplying lost animals or food.
